stories.title: Burnham says UK with Ukraine ‘all the way’ despite ‘outrageous threats’ from Russia – Europe live
stories.summary: Burnham continues by saying that “Ukraine has been Europe’s protector, not a drain on our security, but the frontline of keeping Europe safe.” “That’s why I believe the Ukrainian people deserve not just our continued support, but our gratitude and our respect.” He congratulates Ukraine on its Independence Day on behalf of the UK. He repeats that the UK believes recognises Ukraine’s “independence and sovereignty in full,” and believes that “international borders cannot be changed by force.” He tells “the people of this country, from Lviv to Luhansk,… that we are with you in this struggle all the way, heart and soul.” He says he sees “an unbroken country” in Ukraine, as he pledges continued support for Ukraine. “We will continue to build the 100 year partnership between our two countries, bringing together our cities and our schools, our businesses and our communities, learning from each other and growing together for decades to come. And despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine’s defence.” As he chaired the meeting, Britain’s Andy Burnham has urged Ukraine’s allies to provide more Patriot interceptor missiles to Kyiv, saying the country “needs more help to protect its people right now,” PA agency reported. Speaking in Kyiv as he chaired his first meeting of the “coalition of the willing”, the prime minister said the coalition was “doing everything we can all do and working with our allies outside of this coalition to dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks”. He also called on the US Congress to “ratchet up” economic pressure on Russia. Burnham said Russia’s economy was struggling with a record budget deficit and declining oil revenues as he backed a sanctions bill proposed by the late Republican senator Lindsey Graham.

stories.title: Russia, India discuss cooperation formats on Northern Sea Route
stories.summary: According to Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov, the use of the Arctic route will enable businesses to reduce transportation costs
article_sentences: MOSCOW, August 24.

Rosatom is discussing potential formats for cooperation with India on the Northern Sea Route, Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said at a meeting of the Russian-Indian Intergovernmental Commission on Cooperation.
"State corporation Rosatom is discussing mutually beneficial formats for cooperation with its Indian partners as part of the development of the Northern Sea Route.
Its competitive advantages are clear today, and the use of this Arctic route will enable businesses to reduce transportation costs," he said.

According to Manturov, Rosatom’s experience in building the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant in India also provides a foundation for deeper cooperation in nuclear energy, potentially including new facilities, such as small-scale power generation facilities, as well as the localization of equipment and nuclear fuel production.
Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev said in late 2025 that Russia and India intended to cooperate on the Northern Sea Route.
According to him, this could unlock the potential for around 5 mln metric tons of cargo shipments in both directions.
He said that this transit traffic, which currently passes through the Suez Canal, could instead be routed by the Indian side via the Northern Sea Route.

stories.title: Russia’s top female racquet Andreeva back in WTA Top-5
stories.summary: The Russian, who is playing under a neutral status at international tournaments, now has 5,443 points in the WTA Rankings
article_sentences: WASHINGTON, August 24.
Russia's Mirra Andreeva climbed a spot in this week's WTA (the Women’s Tennis Association) World Rankings, released earlier on Monday.
The Russian, who is playing under a neutral status at international tournaments, now sits 5th in the WTA Rankings with 5,443 points.
Playing last week at the 2026 WTA Cincinnati Open in the United States Andreeva reached the fourth round of the 1,000 class-rated tournament.

This week’s WTA Top-10 is as follows: 1st Aryna Sabalenka (a Belarusian player competing under a neutral status; 8,575 points); 2nd Elena Rybakina (Kazakhstan, 8,141 points); 3rd Jessica Pegula (the United States, 7,265 points); 4th Coco Gauff (the United States, 6,704 points); 5th Mirra Andreeva (a Russian player competing under a neutral status; 5,443 points); 6th Linda Noskova (the Czech Republic, 5,028 points); 7th Karolina Muchova (the Czech Republic, 4,983 points); 8th Iga Swiatek (Poland, 4,809 points); 9th Elina Svitolina (Ukraine, 4,689 points) and 10th Amanda Anisimova (the United States, 4,533 points).
Andreeva, 19, won the French Open in June and is a six-time WTA title holder overall.
In 2023, Andreeva was named WTA rookie of the year.
At the 2024 Paris Olympic Games, she won a silver medal in women’s doubles paired with Diana Shnaider.

On February 28, 2022, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) issued recommendations to international sports federations to bar athletes from Russia and Belarus from taking part in international tournaments, citing Moscow's special military operation in Ukraine as the reason.
Following the IOC's recommendations in late February 2022, the majority of global sports federations decided to bar athletes from Russia and Belarus from all international sports tournaments.

The International Tennis Federation (ITF) ruled on March 1, 2022 to suspend the membership of the Russian and Belarusian national tennis federations while also canceling all previously scheduled tennis tournaments in the two countries.
On March 14, 2022, the ITF also confirmed its prohibition on the Russian and Belarusian national tennis teams from taking part in the 2022 Davis Cup and 2022 Billie Jean King Cup.

stories.title: Ukrainian politicians see corruption as routine practice, not scandal — media
stories.summary: The Economist expects political infighting to grow in the coming weeks
article_sentences: LONDON, August 24.
Corruption and political turmoil are widespread in Ukraine, with recent investigations showing that officials view abuses of power as routine, British magazine.
The Economist said.
"Corruption is treated not as an exceptional scandal but as routine workflow," the magazine said in an article about an investigation into Irina Mudraya, deputy head of Zelensky’s office.
The magazine described the developments as the biggest challenge to Zelensky’s leadership yet.
The Economist said they come at the worst possible time, as Russian strikes increasingly hit their targets and former Defense Minister Mikhail Fyodorov calls for elections.
The magazine expects political infighting to grow in the coming weeks.
A senior official cited by The Economist said things will go wrong all at once as the weather gets colder in October, adding that many people see some key officials as incompetent.

On August 19, Ukraine’s anti-corruption agencies launched a special operation against a criminal group allegedly led by former and incumbent Ukrainian lawmakers and involving employees of Zelensky’s office.
Various sources reported that the suspects included Irina Mudraya, incumbent Verkhovna Rada (parliament) lawmaker Vadim Stolar and former lawmaker Maxim Mykytas.
On the same day, Zelensky dismissed Mudraya amid the developments.
According to Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau, 751 cases involving 1,555 people had been opened by the end of 2025, while more than 300 others were being investigated.
